references.text: Isaiah's prophecy about the judgment on Tyre, which Jesus alludes to when he mentions Tyre and Sidon as examples of pagan cities under God's judgment.
Ezekiel's prophecy against Sidon, showing that Tyre and Sidon were well-known examples of pagan cities under God's judgment—the same cities Jesus uses for comparison.
Joel speaks about Tyre and Sidon and God's judgment upon them, providing background for Jesus' use of these cities as an example of judgment.
Amos's words of judgment against Tyre for their sins, which form part of the prophetic background to Jesus' mention of Tyre in connection with judgment.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says exactly the same thing: that it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for those cities that have rejected his message.
Jesus continues by comparing Capernaum with Sodom, saying it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment—the same pattern of judgment against cities that reject the gospel.
Jesus uses a similar argument that Gentiles (the people of Nineveh and the queen from the South) will rise up in judgment and condemn that generation which rejected him.
The preceding verse where Jesus says it will be more bearable for Sodom than for the city that rejects the disciples—the context for the judgment he pronounces in verse 14.
The immediately preceding verse where Jesus pronounces woe upon Chorazin and Bethsaida, saying that Tyre and Sidon would have repented, forming the basis for the statement in verse 14.
The following verse where Jesus pronounces judgment on Capernaum, as part of the same sequence of judgments to which verse 14 belongs.
